extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians / graduate students working on Ricci flow and surgery (geometric analysts)
extracted.subtask_description: Justification and precise formulation of the canonical neighborhood assumption and associated noncollapsing/surgery parameters for 3-dimensional Ricci flow with surgery; shows how to choose δ(t), r(t), κ to prevent surgery-time accumulation and obtain compactness of rescaled limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy ε)
rubrics_metrics.description: The solution satisfies the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy ε) on a time interval with a positive function r(t): at points with sufficiently large curvature (relative to r(t)) the neighborhood is, up to the ε-accuracy and appropriate scaling, one of the standard models (ε-neck, ε-cap, or region modeled on the standard/ancient κ-solution) and satisfies the associated gradient and derivative estimates (see 7.3.4, Lemmas 7.3.5–7.3.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a nonincreasing positive function r(t) so that on the considered time interval every high-curvature point has an ε-canonical neighborhood; to extend indefinitely one needs a uniform choice of r_i(t) independent of surgery-step index k. Use the standard solution characterization to compare/approximate surgical regions and ensure neighborhoods are ε-close in C^{[ε^{-1}]} topology.

rubrics_metrics.name: κ-noncollapsed condition (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A surgically modified three-dimensional solution g_{ij}(t), 0 ≤ t < T, is κ-noncollapsed at (x0,t0) on the scales less than ρ if: whenever r < ρ and |Rm(x,t)| ≤ r^{-2} for all (x,t) in the parabolic neighborhood P(x0,t0,r,−r^{2}) (where the solution is defined), then Vol_{t0}(B_{t0}(x0,r)) ≥ κ r^{3}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the precise noncollapsing quantitative condition used throughout (see Lemma 7.4.2). One proves uniform κ-noncollapsing on successive time slabs by appropriate smallness of surgery parameters and by local reduced-volume arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: δ(t)-cutoff surgery requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Every surgery performed at time t ∈ (0,T) must be a δ(t)-cutoff surgery (i.e., performed along δ-necks and with cutoff radius controlled by δ(t)), where the surgery parameter function δ(t) is chosen sufficiently small (eventually via a decreasing sequence δ_j with δ_j < ε^{2}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of sequences (δ_j, r_j, κ_j) controlling time-slab behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Given ε>0 there exist decreasing sequences 0<δ_j�<�... , r_j<ε, and κ_j>0 such that for any surgically modified solution with finite surgeries where each surgery time t uses δ(t) bounded by these δ_j's on the corresponding time slab, then on each time interval [(j-1)ε^{2}, jε^{2}) the solution is κ_j-noncollapsed on all scales < ε and satisfies the canonical neighborhood assumption with r = r_j.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the content of Proposition 7.4.1: choose δ_j small (e.g. < ε^{2}) and r_j, κ_j appropriately; this gives uniform local geometric control on each ε^{2}-time slab and is the mechanism for inductively extending the flow while preventing surgery accumulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissible vs barely admissible space-time curves (and L-length lower bound)
rubrics_metrics.description: A space-time curve is admissible if it stays in the space-time region una�ffected by surgery; it is barely admissible if it lies on the boundary of the set of admissible curves. For any finite L there exists �barδ(L,r,m,ε)>0 such that every barely admissible curve γ that meets a gluing cap (i.e., interacts with surgery) satisfies the length-type lower bound integral_{T0}^{t0} sqrt{t0-t} (R(γ(t),t)+2) + |γ'(t)|^{2} dt ≥ L (inequality (7.4.2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By choosing surgery parameters δ sufficiently small one forces barely admissible curves to have arbitrarily large L-length, which implies minimizing Li-Yau-Perelman geodesics avoid surgery regions (i.e., minimizers are admissible). This is used to apply the reduced-volume/max-principle arguments in presence of surgeries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Li-Yau-Perelman distance and exclusion of non-admissible minimizers
rubrics_metrics.description: If a Li-Yau-Perelman minimizer from (x0,t0) to (x,t) were non-admissible (i.e. passes through surgery regions), then for suitably small δ one gets a large lower bound on the reduced distance l (inequality (7.4.5)), e.g. l ≥ 10 ε^{-1}, which contradicts smallness near τ→0. Thus minimizers must be admissible and live in una�ffected regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion is used to guarantee that Perelman's reduced-volume monotonicity and related maximum-principle arguments remain valid for surgically modified solutions by ensuring minimizers avoid surgical caps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced-volume lower bound via canonical neighborhoods and κ-noncollapsing
rubrics_metrics.description: Given canonical neighborhood control and κ-noncollapsing on an earlier time slab, one can find a point (\bar x,\bar t) along a minimizing curve such that a ball B_{\bar t}(\bar x, θ_1 r_m) is una�ffected by surgery and Perelman's reduced volume of that ball (at an earlier time) is bounded below by a positive constant depending only on κ_m and r_m (see (7.4.9) and following estimates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduced-volume lower bound is a key ingredient to derive a lower bound on ordinary volume of spatial balls at later times (thus proving κ-noncollapsing persists across slabs). One uses admissibility of geodesics plus Jacobian comparison and local monotonicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent accumulation of surgery times (two-part strategy)
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid surgery-time accumulation: (1) choose successive surgery parameters δ_{m+1} small enough to 'push surgical regions to infinity' under rescaling; (2) show solutions are smooth on small but uniform time intervals (on compact subsets) so Hamilton's compactness theorem and interior derivative estimates apply (Shi estimates require smoothness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both small δ and uniform short-time smoothness are needed to take limits of rescaled surgical solutions and preclude accumulation of surgery times; these choices underpin the inductive proof of Proposition 7.4.1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local curvature and gradient estimates in canonical neighborhoods
rubrics_metrics.description: In canonical neighborhoods one has quantitative curvature and gradient/derivative estimates (e.g., (7.3.4) style bounds) which imply: if R(y,\hat t) is bounded relative to a scale then on a corresponding parabolic neighborhood the curvature is uniformly controlled and higher derivative estimates (Shi) apply; also neighborhoods are ε-close (in C^{[ε^{-1}]}) to the standard solution after scaling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These estimates are the local analytic control used to extend solutions in time (Assertions 1–3), to compare regions to the standard model, and to ensure compactness of sequences after rescaling; when verifying canonical neighborhoods one repeatedly uses such gradient estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximation by the standard solution (caps/necks characterization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gluing caps and adjacent δ-necks (where surgery is performed) are, after appropriate scaling (by the local cutoff radius h^{-1}), δ'-close to corresponding subsets of the standard solution; conversely, if a point's neighborhood violates the canonical neighborhood assumption then after rescaling it must show a strong ε-neck or ε-cap structure contradicting the choice of violation point (arguments in Step 2, Claims 1–2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Lemmas 7.3.5 and 7.3.6 to conclude that neighborhood structures near surgery regions approximate the standard solution; choosing δ' ≪ ε and working with suitably large cut-off radii gives contradictions to alleged violations of canonical neighborhoods, proving the required uniform structure.
